content: A foaming agent is a type of surfactant that, even in small quantities, promotes the formation of foam or improves the stability of foam by preventing the merging of bubbles. Sodium laureth sulfate (SLES), also known as sodium lauryl ether sulfate, is a widely used detergent and surfactant found in various personal care products such as soaps, shampoos, and toothpaste. It is both cost-effective and highly efficient in producing foam. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), also referred to as sodium dodecyl sulfate, and ammonium lauryl sulfate (ALS) are frequently used as alternatives to SLES in consumer products. In addition to surfactants, a foaming agent can also refer to a substance that releases gas under specific conditions, typically at high temperatures, to create foam from a liquid. For instance, powdered titanium hydride is employed as a foaming agent in the production of metal foams. When exposed to elevated temperatures, it decomposes to release titanium and hydrogen gas, facilitating foam formation. Similarly, zirconium(II) hydride serves a comparable purpose in metal foam production.
